articles.title: Uganda's King Oyo: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
articles.summary: King Oyo ascended to the throne of Uganda's Tooro kingdom when he was just three years old.
articles.body:
A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minster announced.

Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father.

The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US.

Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.

Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch , ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.

Announcing his death, Tooro's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki called his passing on Thursday an "immeasurable loss" to the royal family and the people of Tooro.

"I call upon all the people of Tooro to remain united, calm and prayerful during this profoundly difficult time," Akiiki said on Friday. "May His Majesty the King rest in eternal peace."

The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.

Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured".

"His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.

When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.

The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.

The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.

Similarly, the Rwenzururu Kingdom also extended its condolences to "all those mourning this great loss", according to local media reports.

Others have also paid their respects to the late king.

The Federation of Uganda Football Associations, honoured King Oyo as a "true friend of the beautiful game", and announced a moment of silence before the kick-off of all matches until 4 September in memory of his "legacy, love, passion and contribution" to the sport.

Government minister Margaret Muhanga described the mood in the kingdom as "sombre... you can't see anyone smiling".

The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".

Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.

Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"

Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

articles.title: PA activists face ‘terror’ charges over Trump golf resort protest: Report
articles.summary: Protesters targeted Trump’s Ayrshire resort with red paint and slogans saying ‘Gaza is not 4 sale’.
articles.body:
Palestine Action activists accused of vandalising a Scottish golf course owned by United States President Donald Trump have been accused of “terrorism” offences, according to reports.

The potential use of “terror-scale” sentencing was reported by The Guardian and The New York Times on Friday. The seven activists, who spray-painted messages in support of Gaza and dug up turf at Trump’s Turnberry golf resort in Ayrshire last year, have been charged with malicious damage “having a terrorist connection,” the newspapers reported.

An initial hearing on the cases is due to open at the High Court in Glasgow on Monday, August 31.

The charges stem from a March 8, 2025 protest targeting the resort over Trump’s stance on Gaza. Activists from the British group sprayed red paint across the clubhouse, damaged turf and sprinklers, applied weedkiller to the greens, and painted “Gaza is not 4 sale” across the property.

All seven defendants were charged under ordinary criminal law for malicious property damage. However, the prosecution’s 16-page indictment asserts the acts were “aggravated by reason of having a terrorist connection”.

Palestine Action has been locked in a legal battle with the United Kingdom since the British government proscribed it as a “terrorist” group last year.

Cofounder Huda Ammori said that the charges against those involved in the protest at Turnberry made it clear that prosecutors were trying to appease Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

“We used direct action protests to save lives – the opposite of terrorism – by disrupting the flow of arms being used to murder Palestinians,” she said in a statement.

“By hitting the profits of arms companies and by daring to spray paint on the golf course owned by the demagogue who has enabled Netanyahu’s crimes, we made powerful enemies. The British government chose to appease them by criminalising us as ‘terrorists’,” she added.

Earlier this week, the United States imposed sanctions on Palestine Action and the pro-Palestine international movement Masar Badil, as the administration of President Donald Trump intensifies a global crackdown on critics of Israel.

The US Department of the Treasury also imposed financial penalties on Wednesday against Autistici Inventati, an Italian group that provides digital services to left-wing organisations, including pro-Palestine groups.

John McDonnell, a Labour member of the British parliament and former shadow chancellor of the exchequer, criticised the potential “terror” link in the charges.

“The news that the protesters who allegedly sprayed red paint on Trump’s golf course could face terrorist sentencing, coupled with Trump himself now announcing that he is following Britain’s lead by proscribing Palestine Action as a ‘terrorist’ group, is profoundly embarrassing for Britain,” he said.

“Andy Burnham has inherited this mess from the previous government. This must be the wake-up call to drop this absurdly authoritarian ban, before Starmer’s blueprint is adopted by repressive governments around the world to criminalise protest and suppress political dissent.”

articles.title: Green Party leader Zack Polanski calls for data centre freeze in England; says they 'guzzle' energy, water
articles.summary: UK News: Green Party leader Zack Polanski urges a moratorium on new data centres in England, citing their excessive water and energy consumption. He calls for stricter regulations and local control over these developments.
articles.body: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called for a freeze on approvals for new data centres in England, arguing that the rapidly expanding industry is putting pressure on water and energy supplies.Polanski said the government should introduce tougher environmental requirements for data centres and give local communities a greater say over whether new facilities are built in their areas. He made the comments while visiting the site of a proposed data centre in East London.“We need to slam the brakes on these energy guzzling, water guzzling data centres,” Polanski told the BBC.He called for a moratorium on new developments, apart from smaller facilities serving local communities. Polanski also criticised the government's decision to classify data centres as critical infrastructure, saying the designation was inappropriate while much of the country was experiencing drought.“At a time when three-quarters of the country is in drought, it is outrageous that these are being considered critical infrastructure,” he said. “To most people critical infrastructure means hospitals, water, electricity. It doesn't mean Artificial Intelligence.”Data centres were designated as critical infrastructure in 2024. The classification provides them additional government support during incidents such as cyber-attacks and extreme weather.The Green Party has argued that the designation could allow data centres to receive priority over households for water during shortages. The government has rejected that suggestion, saying data centres would not automatically receive priority when water supplies are under pressure.The debate comes as England has hundreds of data centres, with many more planned. The BBC last reported that there were about 477 in the country.A large proportion are concentrated in London and the south of England, including areas that are currently officially classified as being in drought.Water consumption varies between data centres depending on factors including their size, cooling systems, design and local climate. Facilities in hotter areas generally require more water to cool their equipment.There is currently no requirement for UK data centres to report how much water they consume. However, the Water Research Centre consultancy estimated in February that data centres in England use about 1.9 billion litres of drinking water each year. That represents roughly 0.2% of the non-household water market.The consultancy said there was a “clear upward trend” in data centre water use.The Party has also cited research by environmental charity Global Action Plan, which estimated that large data centres could consume as much as 1.5 million litres of water a day.Polanski and the Greens want new data centres to be built on brownfield sites and close to renewable energy sources so that they can use renewable power where possible. They are also calling for operators to publish annual figures showing how much water and electricity their facilities consume.The industry's representatives have disputed the suggestion that data centres are placing an undue burden on local water supplies.Mark Acton, executive director of the Data Centre Alliance, said data centres were not taking water away from local communities and used less water than leisure centres and golf courses.Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, Acton said obtaining planning permission for data centres was already “very difficult”, including in areas designated as AI growth zones.“Data centres are not just AI, data centres run our lives... social media runs through data centres, our banking systems run through data centres,” he said. “We depend on these things massively.”The government has opposed Polanski's proposed freeze, warning that halting new developments could affect investment, employment and national security.A government spokesperson said a pause would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad” and leave Britain dependent on overseas computing to process sensitive health and defence data.“Put simply: it would be a disaster for jobs and national security,” the spokesperson said.The government also said its support for data centres did not amount to an unconditional approval of every proposed development.“That said, this does not mean a blank cheque for Big Tech or that every data centre should be approved,” the spokesperson said.“Developers must plan to use clean power, use water responsibly, create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built.”The government has also pointed to water lost through leaks, saying roughly a fifth of the country's water supply is lost in this way.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Popular beach town rejects noise, trash and traffic as it weighs stricter vacation rental rules
articles.summary: Pensacola Beach residents say large vacation rentals sleeping 30-40 guests drive noise, parking and trash problems as officials weigh a strict new registry.
articles.body: A popular Florida beach community is weighing tighter rules for its short-term vacation rentals after full-time residents have raised concerns about visitors' noise, overflowing trash and parking complications. The proposal under consideration for Pensacola Beach could create a registry for vacation rentals. It could require owners to designate someone who can be reached 24/7 when problems arise, according to reports. Rhonda Dorfman, president of Pensacola Beach Advocates and a full-time resident of the island, told Fox News Digital that one concern is giving law enforcement a clear point of contact when complaints are made at rental properties. POPULAR DESTINATION CRACKS DOWN HARD ON TOURISTS AS NEW LIMITS THREATEN SUMMER GETAWAYS "The sheriff's deputies have a very difficult time finding out who's in charge here," Dorfman said, noting that calls can involve complaints about noise and underage drinking. She said many problems are tied to larger vacation homes that can accommodate dozens of guests. "It's not the three- and four-person families that come out to the beach," Dorfman said. Instead, she said, some homes "sleep 30 or 40 people — and that is where we're getting the problems." Large groups can also put pressure on parking and trash collection, she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "If you have a home that sleeps 30 or 40 people, even if you put five people in a car, that's six cars," Dorfman said. Trash left outside between guest checkouts and scheduled collection days has also become a concern, she indicated. "That trash sits out there in the heat. It stinks. It's ugly," she said. Noise can become another issue at night, with Pensacola Beach's noise ordinance taking effect at 10 p.m., according to Dorfman. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Still, she noted that vacationers come to Pensacola Beach to enjoy themselves during the summer. "You work 50 weeks out of the year, you save up for your vacation, and you want to have a good time," she said. "We know you're here on vacation, and we want you to have a wonderful time, but you are in a residential community," Dorfman said. Online discussions reveal the competing perspectives on tourism. Some Reddit commenters have pushed back against criticism of visitors, pointing to the economic activity that tourism brings to the Pensacola area. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Other commenters highlighted the appeal of visiting Pensacola Beach despite its crowds. "The beaches are beautiful," another commenter wrote, while advising travelers to "pack your patience" when the area becomes particularly busy. "We don't want to get rid of short-term rentals." Dorfman emphasized that the residents who support additional rules are not seeking to eliminate vacation rentals. "We don't want to get rid of short-term rentals," she said. "We want our low-density residential communities to still feel like a community." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She said officials are looking at regulations used in other Florida communities, including Gulf Breeze, Anna Maria Island and Panama City, as they consider what could work for Pensacola Beach.

articles.title: After six months of war, what have US, Iran gained and lost?
articles.summary: Many of the US president’s goals remain unfulfilled, despite claims of victory.
articles.body:
It has been six months since February 28, when the US and Israel shocked the world by launching missile strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior Iranian officials in Tehran, as well as scores of children in a school in Minab, southern Iran.

US President Donald Trump then claimed the conflict would only last “four to five weeks”.

In the months since, the war has erupted on several other fronts, reaching as far as the Caspian Sea. It has triggered a global oil supply crisis as the US and Iran battle for control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which more than one-fifth of oil and natural gas cargo transited.

And it has resulted in an estimated 8,000-10,000 deaths, as well as tens of thousands of injuries.

The conflict is also realigning the global order, experts say, as new alliances form and dominant ones show signs of crumbling.

Has the US achieved any of its war objectives?

The US’s goals were not initially clear: officials first claimed the strikes were carried out in preemptive self-defence.

According to demands presented on the eve of the war, and a jumble of sometimes contradictory statements from Trump and senior US defence officials, they include the following:

Despite Trump’s claim that the US had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear capabilities when it joined in at the end of Israel’s 12-day war on Iran in June 2025, the US and Israel again claimed in February that Tehran was just weeks away from developing nuclear weapons.

Repeated strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites during the war have likely caused vast damage to the facilities, but it is believed Tehran still possesses 440kg of highly enriched uranium, which could be used to make a weapon.

The Trump administration wanted Iran to hand over this stock to the US and to commit to zero enrichment of uranium going forward. Iran refused to do this, although at one point appeared open to the possibility of handing the stock over to a third country. Iran also insisted on retaining the capacity to develop a nuclear power programme, which requires much lower levels of uranium enrichment.

Later, Trump briefly floated the idea of US troops retrieving the stock by force – a potentially dangerous mission.

In the June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by both sides, Iran agreed not to pursue a nuclear weapon – something it had always pledged anyway. The MoU unravelled as its vague wording led to disagreements about what it actually stipulated.

Clark Summers, a US military veteran and professor at Belmont Abbey College in North Carolina, said the US “can rightly assert that these ends have been achieved. Although for how long before Iran can rebuild is difficult to assess.”

But Iranian expert and professor at the Australian National University (ANU), Alam Saleh, disagreed, and noted that Iran’s nuclear power programme is still intact. “The US lost even before the war,” he said, adding that the effort also shows that Washington failed in last year’s 12-day war.

On day one of the war – February 28 – the US killed Khamenei alongside several other senior officials. Trump, two days earlier, said regime change is “the best thing that could happen”.

As the US launched missiles, he also called on “Iranian patriots who yearn for freedom to seize this moment to be brave, be bold, be heroic, and take back your country”.

Iran’s political leadership has, however, remained largely the same under the new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei – the late ayatollah’s son.

Summers told Al Jazeera that the goal may have been “ad hoc” or improvised rather than well-planned. But “killing leaders does not mean strategic achievements, even if it’s a tactical success,” Saleh said.

Ending support for regional proxy groups

Iran’s “axis of resistance” is an umbrella comprising a number of armed groups around the region that it funds. This includes Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen, Hamas in the Gaza Strip, and several smaller groups in Iraq and Syria.

There are no signs that Tehran’s support for them has ended, and this demand did not appear in the MoU signed by the US.

Hezbollah went to war with Israel in Iran’s defence, and Iran has refused to negotiate an end to the war unless the Lebanon front is included. The Houthis, meanwhile, have launched a blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, partly in support of Iran.

Washington swore it would “raze” Iran’s missile facilities to the ground when it launched the war on February 28. The US also pledged to destroy Iran’s navy.

Trump has since claimed that about 82 percent of Iran’s missiles are gone and the navy is degraded.

In April, he also said that 158 Iranian naval vessels had been hit, while US Central Command (CENTCOM) has continued to announce dozens of strikes on command centres of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Iran, however, has continued to fire missiles, most recently launching a long-range missile in July that killed three US soldiers in Jordan.

Furthermore, the demand for an end to Iran’s ballistic missiles programme was also absent from the July MoU.

In June, Trump said the US would seize and control Iran’s Kharg island , the heart of Iranian oil production.

To date, the US does not control any Iranian territory.

What have the US and Iran gained and lost during the war?

Besides the US demands at the start of the war, several other pressure points have emerged during the conflict.

Soon after the war began, Iran in effect closed the narrow but critical Strait of Hormuz, which passes through its territorial waters as well as those of Oman. Since then, shipping traffic has slumped from more than 100 ships per day to an average of about five.

To enforce this closure, Iran began striking vessels in the strait, the only route to the open ocean for Gulf oil and gas producers, which had not gained its explicit permission to pass through.

The US responded with its own naval blockade on Iranian ports in and around the strait. This is continuing.

Despite a large number of expletive-laden demands from Trump since then – many of them on social media – that Tehran reopen the strait, Iran has not budged. It is currently negotiating plans for the future of the waterway, through which more than one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies were shipped before the war, with Oman.

As part of these negotiations, Iran announced this week that it has agreed to a shipping route, which it will partially control, with Oman.

While Trump has recently claimed that the US has “full control” of the strait and that it is open to vessels, shipping remains at an all-time low and Iran has continued to fire at any vessels trying to pass without its permission.

Iran sees the strait as its main piece of leverage in the war with the US, which Salah said, Iran views as an “existential threat”.

Iran: The war’s impact on Iran’s economy has been severe. The Iranian rial has in effect collapsed . Food prices have surged amid the war, and the US blockade and renewed sanctions have hampered Iranian oil exports, with the blockade cutting oil revenue by at least $6bn. Tehran’s economy has long been battered by US sanctions, although the fragile ceasefire provided temporary relief. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said last week that economic pressure is a “rerun we know by heart” and that the country knows how to survive it.

US: US consumers have also felt the pressure of the war at the petrol pump, making the conflict highly unpopular. A July poll by The Associated Press revealed that two-thirds of Americans are against the conflict. While many tend to forget there’s a war, Summers said, they do remember it acutely when petrol prices rise. In states like California, gasoline prices doubled. That anger will likely translate into a political backlash against Republicans in November’s midterms, experts say.

Iran: Iran’s targeting of US military assets as well as both military and nonmilitary infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states and Jordan has not made it popular regionally, experts note. Iran has hit infrastructure in Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain. Those states have called this a violation of their sovereignty. However, Iran’s economic and political ties with China have held, as Beijing has managed a delicate dance by advocating against sanctions on Iran while refraining from becoming fully entangled in the conflict. Trade relations with Russia also remain strong.

US: The US has faced reluctance from its NATO allies to back it up in this war. Despite being asked directly by Trump, they have refused to join the war. Spain and Italy, in particular, have highly criticised the conflict, while Germany, Israel’s strongest ally in Europe, has done the same. France rejected calls to send warships to enforce the blockade. Gulf allies, Pakistan and Turkiye have all similarly refused, while in Asia, Japan, Australia and South Korea all declined to get involved. Gulf allies are also likely weighing the fact that it is the US’s war on Iran which has caused them to become targets.

Iran: US experts say that claims Washington has degraded Iran’s military capabilities are correct. Several army bases have been struck while Iran’s ballistic missile stockpiles are down by about 82 percent, according to Trump. However, Iran is still launching missiles and, while nuclear facilities have been damaged, it still has possession of its enriched uranium stockpile. Experts point out that Iran likely has a bigger appetite for an atomic weapon now than before the war began. Tehran has also continued to produce and deploy its mass-produced, cheap Shahed drones. An estimated 1,221 military personnel were killed by April, although the real toll is likely higher.

US: The US has lost 18 soldiers and more than 750 have been wounded. That’s “quite low”, Summers said. However, US media reports suggest the Pentagon has severely depleted stockpiles of some of its most powerful and most expensive weapons – particularly its Patriot defence missiles – something Washington denies. Those missiles are only produced in the dozens annually and cost millions of dollars each. In August, the US signed a $22.9bn deal with manufacturer Raytheon to boost Tomahawk cruise missile production from 60 to more than 1,000 annually.

“Both of them have not achieved anything,” Saleh of ANU said, noting that the US has failed to translate military superiority to actual gains despite being a “superpower” fighting a “middle power”.

China and Russia are likely observing Washington’s weaknesses, making new military calculations in the event of a future conflict with the US, he said. That has implications for Taiwan, especially as the US has now deployed its last aircraft carrier in the Pacific to the Middle East. The shift leaves the US without an aircraft carrier in the Western Pacific, despite Washington’s previous strategic emphasis on the region.

“Iran surviving also does not mean it’s a winner,” however, Saleh said. “This might be a defeat for the US, but it’s not a victory for Iran either.”

articles.title: More delay: AMCA programme timeline reset as ADA grants more time for proposals
articles.summary: News News: The Aeronautical Development Agency has extended the submission deadline for one of India's most closely watched defence programmes, giving industry b.
articles.body: The Aeronautical Development Agency has extended the submission deadline for one of India's most closely watched defence programmes, giving industry bidders two additional months to file their proposals for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft. The revised deadline is now October 30, pushed back from the original August 27 cutoff, with bids scheduled to be formally opened a day later, on October 31.The tender, floated in May this year for a programme valued at around Rs 15,000 crore, invited private industry to compete for the role of Development-cum-Production Partner on India's indigenous fifth-generation stealth fighter. Bidders had originally been given a tight 60-day window to respond, but sources indicate the extension came after companies in the fray sought additional time to put together comprehensive proposals for a project of this scale and complexity.Three consortia are currently in contention for the AMCA contract - Tata Advanced Systems, Larsen & Toubro along with Bharat Electronics Limited, and a grouping involving Bharat Forge and Bharat Earth Movers Limited. The L&T-BEL combination has already brought aerostructures specialist Dynamatic Technologies on board as an exclusive partner, aiming to combine L&T's systems integration expertise with BEL's strength in defence electronics.The stakes attached to this bid are considerable. Under the terms of the RFP, whichever partner is selected will be required to achieve the AMCA's first prototype flight within 30 months of signing the contract, an extremely tight timeline for a fifth-generation stealth aircraft programme. The winning bidder will also need to complete 1,800 test sorties across five separate prototypes within a firm 84-month window, roughly seven years, from the date of the agreement.The urgency is tied directly to the Indian Air Force's own planning, with the service aiming to induct its first AMCA squadrons by the mid-2030s. The IAF eventually plans to field around seven squadrons of the aircraft, beginning with the Mk-1 variant powered by American GE-F414 engines, before transitioning to a more powerful Mk-2 version equipped with a jointly developed 110 kN engine.By placing private industry at the centre of manufacturing rather than routing everything through DRDO's traditional public-sector channels, the government is betting on faster prototyping, more agile supply chains, and better production efficiency, key ingredients if India hopes to join the small club of nations capable of designing and building a fifth-generation fighter on its own timeline.

articles.title: Gatwick Airport facing water outage after main burst in Horley
articles.summary: SES Water says it has repaired a burst main which was affecting supply to the airport.
articles.body:
Gatwick Airport passengers were left without water after a main burst in a nearby field.

SES Water said that it located a burst main in Horley, with parts of the airport left without water as a result.

A spokesperson for the airport confirmed that the issue had affected water supply in both terminals and was under investigation by SES Water. The water company said it had begun to restore supply and that water pressure was beginning to return to normal.

Flights remained unaffected by the disruption, the airport added.

The issues come after a major supply outage in July saw passengers face long queues for toilets at the West Sussex airport, with restaurants and bars also closing.

Natasha Nzekwe, who was due to fly to Amsterdam from the North Terminal, said: "It's quite frustrating, but everyone seems to be pretty fine.

"There's no water at all, you can't even wash your hands in the toilets.

"If I were on a long haul flight I think it would be worse, not being able to properly wash your hands is frustrating, and they haven't given us any information as to what is going on."

Naduni Abeywickrama, who was travelling from London to Aberdeen, added that the delay was "extremely frustrating".

She added: "No one seems to be making a scene, but I feel frustrated because this is the second time this has happened."

Toilets in the airport's North Terminal are closed as a result of the supply issue, while the majority of toilets in the South Terminal are unaffected.

Food outlets in the North Terminal remain open, but for passenger seating only.

Anthony Rochester, head of networks at SES Water, said that it "had restored water supplies to Gatwick Airport and the surrounding areas by re-routing our network".

"We're continuing to work closely with the airport as we understand water isn't yet flowing throughout their buildings", he added.

A Gatwick Airport spokesperson said: "Toilets have remained available throughout, and food and beverage outlets are now reopening and serving hot food.

"Since becoming aware of the issue, we have been working closely with our airport partners to help minimise the impact and successfully ensure all of today's flights continue to depart as scheduled.

"We recognise the inconvenience caused by today's water shortage and thank passengers for their patience and understanding. We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

In July, both terminals at Gatwick Airport lost running water for several hours after a power failure at a treatment works in the area.

articles.title: US ICE agency to spend $16.7m on electric shock gloves
articles.summary: The much-criticised immigration agency has agreed a contract for 6,000 pairs of gloves that will deliver painful shocks.
articles.body:
The United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency is to spend $16.7m on 6,000 pairs of electric-shock gloves.

A notice on a federal database published on Thursday showed that the much-maligned agency, which has been the face of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has agreed a no-bid contract with Kentucky-based firm Compliant Technologies for the supply of the gloves, alongside support equipment and services, over the next six months.

ICE stated in its procurement notice that the “de-escalation devices” will be used when dealing with detainees and protesters.

Officers will deploy the equipment in “high-tension environments”, including during arrests, while transporting combative detainees, and when managing civil disturbances outside detention facilities, the agency said.

“It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties.”

The agency said the shocks would help officers handle aggressive inmates, prevent escape attempts, force people to expose hidden hands for handcuffing, and manage crowds.

ICE added that the gloves offer an alternative to “more severe force” such as firearms, noting they would be used under “approved policy, training, and accountability standards”.

The agency has concluded the contract despite mounting opposition from civil rights advocates and Democratic lawmakers, who contend officers cannot be trusted to use the technology responsibly.

Critics note that ICE officers already face intense criticism over their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing Trump’s immigration policies.

The American Civil Liberties ⁠Union said giving immigration agents “a concealed means of ⁠delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability”.

Fatal shootings by ICE agents of two ⁠US citizens in Minnesota earlier this year spurred protests and widespread criticism. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody nationwide since Trump took office.

The procurement notice was posted hours after a group of US senators urged the agency to scrap the purchase in a letter to its acting director.

“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant scepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter read.

The lawmakers warned the technology carries “substantial risks” during civil arrests if deployed without clear limits, proper training, and independent oversight. They called on ICE to publicly disclose how officers will be trained and how the use of the gloves will be documented and internally reviewed.

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, dismissed the criticism.

“Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers,” the agency said in a statement.

articles.title: Flock CEO Garrett Langley's address leaked online after he urged Americans to 'compromise' between privacy and safety
articles.summary: US News: Flock CEO Garrett Langley emerged as the most controversial personality of this month as his surveillance technology company is facing massive backlas.
articles.body: Flock CEO Garrett Langley emerged as the most controversial personality of this month as his surveillance technology company is facing massive backlash because of the huge scope of misuse of the technology. It is not confirmed whether the address shared online is Langley's real address. Many social media users shared a screenshot of a blurred Google map and claimed that Langley got his house blurred on Google map while asking Americans to compromise on privacy.What is the controversy over Flock cameras?Flock, according to the company, is designed to help authorized users find relevant evidence for investigations without compromising safety and compliance. Flock cameras can read license plates and they can record and analyze everything that passes them.But instances of misusing this technology are plenty. A Kentucky police officer was arrested after authorities said he used the Flock Safety license plate reader camera system to track his ex-girlfriend over 2,000 times.Protesters vandalized these traffic cameras as people are waking up to the threat of the new tech and some cities have canceled their Flock contracts.Langley acknowledged the initial loopholes and said they were working on it, but Americans must compromise on their compromise when it is a question of safety, he said. “When people talk about just one of these, privacy or safety, they’re prioritizing the wrong thing, and what we have to prioritize as a country is compromise,” Langley said in the interview. “How do we have our safety, and how do we balance privacy?”"I value my privacy. My family values their privacy. My employees value their privacy. But what we are talking about is safety as well," he said adding that cars have never been banned because they cause accidents.Senator launches investigation into FlockSen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), the chair of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, has launched an investigation into Flock Safety’s national surveillance network and is demanding to know who has access to the personal data of Americans captured on Flock cameras. “The overwhelming majority of Americans captured in those records did nothing wrong. articles.title: Dutch court hands life sentence to Rwandan man for genocide role
articles.summary: Eugene N. was convicted for his part in a massacre at a stadium in which 3,000 Tutsis were slaughtered.
articles.body:
A Dutch court has sentenced a Rwandan man to life in prison for his role in the murder of thousands during the 1994 genocide in the Central African country.

The Hague district court found Eugene N guilty of war crimes and genocide on Friday, and issued the sentence.

Judges called his conduct a “significant lack of respect for human dignitiy and for human life,” and said that only a life sentence would serve justice “to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families”.

Named only as Eugene N, the suspect helped ransack and burn homes in two mostly Tutsi communities, before taking part in a mob that descended on roughly 3,000 Tutsis sheltering in a stadium in Mbazi in April of 1994.

He directed the Hutu attackers to let no one escape and threw a grenade into the crowd, the court said. Survivors of the initial attack were later beaten and hacked to death.

Eugene N, variously reported to be 66 or 67 years old, fled the Netherlands in 1998 and later became a Dutch citizen. Rwanda sought his extradition in 2014, but the Netherlands’ law shields nationals from being handed over.

Prosecutors opened their case in 2020, questioning more than 30 witnesses before arresting him in 2024.

Eugene N denied his involvement, his defence portraying him as having tried to stop the violence and lost dozens of relatives himself. His representatives called him “a broken man”.

Prosectutors countered, “If the horrific crimes of the suspect … do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?”

Rwanda’s 1994 genocide killed more 800,000 people, mostly Tutsis, in roughly three months of violence directed by Hutu ethnonationalist leaders.

A United Nations tribunal prosecuted leading organisers, but European courts have since pursued lower-level suspects under universal jurisdiction, which allows atrocities and war crimes to be prosecuted regardless of where they occurred.

Dutch courts have convicted other genocide suspects, and in some cases, extradited them to Rwanda.

articles.title: Qatar pledges support for efforts to end Libya’s political division
articles.summary: Qatari minister meets army chief amid efforts to bridge longstanding political divisions in Libya.
articles.body:
Qatar’s minister of state has pledged his country’s commitment to ending longstanding political division in Libya during a visit to Benghazi.

Minister of State Mohammed bin Abdulaziz al-Khulaifi met with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the self-styled Libyan National Army, which is aligned with the unrecognised eastern-based government, on Thursday.

Libya has been split since 2014 between the Tripoli-based government of National Unity, led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and the Haftar-backed eastern administration of Osama Hammad.

The visit, during which al-Khulaifi expressed Qatar’s support for Libyan unity and sovereignty, comes as the country faces the challenge of implementing a recently agreed election pact.

The two officials discussed regional developments and “topics of common interest,” the Qatari Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Al-Khulaifi affirmed Qatar’s support for “a political process that reflects Libyans’ aspirations while aiming at preserving the country’s sovereignty,” according to the statement.

He also stressed the need for continued dialogue and reconciliation to build consensus and pave the way for stability.

Qatar will keep engaging with Libyan parties and leaders to back United Nations efforts towards a political agreement, al-Khulaifi added.

He earlier told Al Jazeera he had discussed ways to support the political process and national dialogue with leaders in Tripoli.

Libyan negotiators agreed last week to an initial election pact aimed at ending years of political division within the country.

A document obtained by Al Jazeera Arabic shows the “4+4” committee’s deal , initiated in Tunisia, rewrites the laws governing presidential and legislative elections and sets a 24-month deadline to hold them.

The committee drew four members each from the eastern House of Representatives and the Tripoli-linked High Council of the State.

The pact, however, is on shaky ground, with people from both sides saying they were left out of talks or had not seen the final text.

The United Nations labelled the deal an important step and says the full agreement will be published once it is formally signed.

The UN and other mediators have spent years trying to resolve the split by arranging elections. However, the implementation of the pact is viewed as challenging, due to divided state institutions, legal voids, and lingering political mistrust.

Libyan legal expert Al-Mahdi Kashbour told Al Jazeera that there appears to be a gap between the powers of the parties that signed the agreement and the institutions with the authority to implement it.

Libya political analyst Elias al-Barouni stressed that the pact does not make any concrete plans for the country’s elections. Even if legal hurdles are cleared, the problem then shifts to who governs Libya in the interim, he added.

articles.title: In 2024, a Colorado county paid $34 million for a 650-acre ranch privately owned for more than a century; 2 years later, 530 acres are being transferred into the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness
articles.summary: US News: In a major expansion of protected public land, 530 acres of a historic Colorado mountain ranch are being formally added to the Maroon Bells-Snowmass W.
articles.body: In a major expansion of protected public land, 530 acres of a historic Colorado mountain ranch are being formally added to the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness, two years after local officials secured the property in a record $34 million purchase. Known as Snowmass Falls Ranch, the 650-acre property sits in the upper Snowmass Creek Valley and had been privately owned for more than a century. Pitkin County bought the property in 2024 through its Open Space and Trails programme to prevent it from being divided for housing. Under the planned agreement, most of the ranch will be transferred to the United States Forest Service and permanently added to the surrounding 181,535-acre federal wilderness area. The transfer completes a decades-long effort by conservationists to protect the environmentally sensitive valley floor, which lies at the foot of the Elk Mountains.A century of private ownershipBefore European settlement, the land was part of the historic territory of the Ute People. In the early 20th century, Danish immigrant Kate Lindvig put together several parcels through the Homestead Act and direct purchases. She became known as the "Cattle Queen of Snow Mass". Lindvig ran the ranch on her own until 1943, when she sold it to Bob Perry, his wife Ruth Brown Perry and her brother, D.R.C. Brown, Jr. The Perry family looked after the property for nearly 80 years before eventually putting it on the market. The ranch was listed for sale in 2021 for $50 million. With property prices rising rapidly in Pitkin County, local conservation groups feared that the rare, connected stretch of land could be divided into expensive luxury homes. “Snowmass Falls Ranch is quite easily the most extraordinary piece of private land in Pitkin County,” said Dale Will, acquisition and projects director for Pitkin County Open Space and Trails, during public discussions about the proposal. “We've held our breath since the property was listed, but never gave up on the hope that the ranch could be preserved”.Financing the record purchaseThe $34 million purchase was the largest open space acquisition in Pitkin County’s history, doubling the previous record of $17 million paid for Sky Mountain Park in 2010. The county financed the deal through open space bonds issued in 2020, along with a $10 million loan from Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO). The organisation distributes state lottery money to support conservation projects by local governments. Additional help came from The Wilderness Land Trust, which worked with local officials on the federal land transfer process. According to local news outlet The Slope, official records published through Pitkin County’s civic alert portal and financial information from Alpine Bank, the deal was designed to allow the county to sell a large part of the ranch to the federal government later. The county plans to transfer 530 acres into the White River National Forest using money from the Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF). This will allow Pitkin County to recover a significant part of the money it spent buying the property. The remaining 120 acres contain historic farm buildings and basic cabins. These will remain under county control or be protected through a conservation easement to preserve the land and maintain future public access.Protecting important wildlife habitatThe ranch is surrounded on three sides by federally protected wilderness and contains a range of habitats, including beaver ponds, spruce forests, alpine wetlands and large aspen groves. The property also has two miles of frontage along Snowmass Creek and holds senior water rights that are important for agricultural and municipal supplies downstream. The land provides important summer habitat for native wildlife, including elk, mule deer, moose, black bears and mountain lions. It also contains two natural waterfalls, including Snowmass Falls, which gives the ranch its name. The property is also important for outdoor recreation. Two major U.S. Forest Service trails cross the ranch, giving hikers and backpackers routes into the Maroon Bells-Snowmass area. With the land now under county ownership and being transferred to federal protection, public access to the trailheads will be secured permanently, ending long-running access concerns near the entrance. Gary Tennenbaum, director of Pitkin County Open Space and Trails, described the acquisition as an important moment for conservation in the county during the early stages of the purchase. “The final pieces of major public land in Pitkin County that we haven't been able to conserve are out there, and this was one of them, and it was a big one,” Tennenbaum noted. “We hope to transfer most of the ranch to the Forest Service as soon as possible, but for now, this amazing property will be open space”. With 530 acres now moving into federal management, the former private property will receive permanent protection under the Wilderness Act. The move ensures that the upper valley floor will remain undeveloped and open to the public for generations to come.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UK has billions in contracts with firms tied to illegal Israeli settlements
articles.summary: Al Jazeera investigation reveals UK public money flowing to companies linked to Israeli settlements in occupied land.
articles.body:
At least 17 companies linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank hold United Kingdom public-sector contracts worth more than 2.1 billion pounds ($2.85bn), an Al Jazeera investigation reveals.

The findings come as more than 140 UK Labour MPs are calling on the government to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements, a move Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering.

Our analysis of procurement records, company filings and corporate disclosures found that businesses named by the United Nations over their involvement in illegal Israeli settlements – and companies those businesses ultimately own or control as subsidiaries – have secured contracts across the British public sector, including in areas such as road maintenance, transport, emergency services and driving licensing.

“Evidence is growing that the UK may be in breach of its international obligations … by continuing to contract with entities identified by the UN as providing assistance of this sort,” Stephen Humphreys, professor of international law at the London School of Economics, told Al Jazeera.

Data compiled by public procurement analysts Tussell, and shared with Al Jazeera, shows the 17 companies and entities hold 125 public-sector contracts with a combined award value of 2.129 billion pounds ($2.89bn).

Companies owned by Motorola Solutions, the United States technology and communications giant, account for more than 1.7 billion pounds ($2.3bn) of the total – the vast majority through its British subsidiary Airwave Solutions. Other contracts we reviewed are held by firms within four other corporate groups including Heidelberg Materials, a German multinational building materials company; the French engineering group Egis; the Spanish train manufacturer CAF and Chinese conglomerate Fosun.

A report by the United Nations Human Rights Office identifies the five corporate groups as involved in business activities related to illegal Israeli settlements.

Heidelberg Materials’ Israeli subsidiary owns a quarry on Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank, while Motorola is embedded in the security infrastructure of illegal settlements. Egis and CAF are involved in Jerusalem’s expanding light-rail network – a project activists say entrenches Israel’s control by integrating settlements into the city while further fragmenting Palestinian neighbourhoods.

Fosun International, whose subsidiary Breas Medical receives UK public money, also owns the controversial Israeli cosmetics manufacturer Ahava , which operates in the Mitzpe Shalem illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank. Civil rights groups, including the Palestinian Solidarity Campaign in the UK, decry Ahava as a firm that is “complicit” in the theft of Palestinian land and livelihoods.

Meanwhile, violence is escalating in the occupied West Bank.

In July 2024, the International Court of Justice found Israel’s continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful and said it must end “as rapidly as possible”. The court also placed obligations on other states “not to render aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by Israel’s illegal presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory”.

That raises questions over Britain’s continued commercial relationships with the companies identified in Al Jazeera’s investigation, observers said.

‘UK government is propping up apartheid’

Humphreys believes that Britain may also be failing to meet its legal obligations by “failing to launch its own investigation into their activities, with a view to preventing them if necessary”.

The UK has also warned businesses against bidding for construction tenders in illegal settlements.

“Businesses should not consider bidding for construction tenders,” a government statement issued this month said, warning of “legal and reputational consequences” and the risk of involvement in “serious breaches of international law”.

Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn said Al Jazeera’s findings expose a contradiction between the UK’s stated position and its economic ties.

“Quite simply, the UK government is propping up apartheid,” Corbyn told Al Jazeera. “Every day, the UK deepens its complicity in Israel’s economy of occupation and, in turn, Israel’s economy of genocide.”

The Cabinet Office told Al Jazeera that individual public authorities make decisions to exclude suppliers case-by-case for each contract. It said public procurement in the UK should not be used to boycott suppliers linked to other countries unless formal UK sanctions, embargoes or restrictions are in place.

Here’s what we found about some of the companies involved in settlement trade:

Motorola Solutions: Tech embedded in illegal settlements

The UN identifies Motorola in connection with two settlement-related activities: the “supply of security services, equipment and materials to enterprises operating in settlements” and the “provision of services and utilities supporting the maintenance and existence of settlements, including transport”.

Al Jazeera contacted the Motorola Solutions group for comment but received no response.

It is the largest beneficiary of UK public money that we investigated.

Motorola’s subsidiaries are entrusted with providing communications equipment to the emergency services in the UK. The largest contract identified by Al Jazeera is held by Airwave Solutions, a Motorola subsidiary. The Home Office awarded Airwave an extension worth 1.562 billion pounds ($2.13bn) to provide the secure communications network used by police, fire and ambulance services across England, Scotland and Wales. Motorola Solutions UK separately holds contracts worth 123.9 million pounds ($170m), including a 36.5-million-pound ($49.8m) Ministry of Defence contract for Airwave radios, accessories and airtime.

Five companies now ultimately controlled by Motorola Solutions Inc – Airwave Solutions Ltd, Motorola Solutions UK Ltd, CRFS Ltd, 3TC Software Ltd and Noggin IT Ltd – hold 91 active UK public-sector contracts worth 1.726 billion pounds ($2.3bn), according to the latest Tussell data.

Motorola Solutions Inc and its Israeli subsidiary, Motorola Solutions Israel Ltd, were included when the UN Human Rights Office first published its database of businesses involved in specified settlement-related activities in 2020. Both remain in its latest version.

Official records provide a glimpse of how the company’s technology has been embedded in settlements.

Tenders from Mateh Binyamin Regional Council and the municipal corporation of Ariel, both illegal settlements, show Motorola command-and-control technology being used in security and surveillance infrastructure.

Motorola equipment has also been bought by the Israeli Civil Administration, the military body through which Israel administers civilian affairs in the occupied West Bank.

In 2005, the UN reported that Motorola supplied surveillance systems to settlements including Hebron, Karmei Tzur and Bracha.

Motorola’s relationship with the Israeli authorities continues today. An Israeli government procurement document obtained by Al Jazeera shows Motorola Solutions Israel was awarded a 25.5-million-shekel ($8.7m) contract in May 2026 to maintain approximately 19,000 police radios and provide encryption licences until April 2028.

Heidelberg Materials: A controversial quarry on occupied land

The UN has listed Heidelberg Materials over the commercial use of natural resources in occupied Palestinian territory.

In Britain, five Heidelberg Materials companies hold 25 public-sector contracts worth 184.79 million pounds ($252m). Almost all of that – 179.03 million pounds ($244m) – is held by Hanson Quarry Products Europe Ltd. Its contracts include 60 million pounds ($81.9m) from Westmorland and Furness Council for road surfacing and highway works between 2024 and 2027, and a 50-million-pound ($68.3m) surfacing maintenance contract with Somerset Council.

Its Israeli subsidiary, Hanson Israel, owns the Nahal Raba quarry, south of Qalqilya in the West Bank. The quarry sits on land belonging to the Palestinian villages of az-Zawiya and Rafat, according to Who Profits.

An official Civil Administration planning notice reviewed by Al Jazeera shows a proposal was approved to expand the site.

Who Profits, a group that researches links between the private sector and the economy in the Israeli-occupied territories, said the approval was granted on May 28, 2025.

Heidelberg told Al Jazeera that in 2023, Hanson Israel “ceased all activities at the Nahal Raba quarry and the associated asphalt plant and ready-mix concrete plant”, adding that only security personnel are present on site.

Egis: Selling transport infrastructure that supports settlements

French engineering group Egis provides another type of connection via transport infrastructure linking illegal Israeli settlements in occupied East Jerusalem with the rest of the city.

The UN lists Egis in connection with the “provision of services and utilities supporting the maintenance and existence of settlements, including transport”.

Egis’s own material shows that its involvement in Jerusalem’s expanding light-rail network continues today, with the company website advertising a job for an engineering expert based in Jerusalem on its light-rail projects.

Jerusalem Transportation Master Plan procurement documents from 2017 also identify Egis Rail as its general consultant, responsible for supervising and coordinating planning and design work on the Blue and Green lines.

Jerusalem’s light rail crosses into occupied East Jerusalem and links illegal Israeli settlements there with West Jerusalem. UN reports have described the railway as “additional infrastructure serving the illegal settlement network” and said it further isolates occupied East Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied West Bank.

Egis told Al Jazeera it “formally expressed its disagreement with this inclusion” in the UN database.

In Britain, five companies and entities controlled by Egis hold six public-sector contracts worth 133.60 million pounds ($182.4m). Almost the entire amount comes from a single contract, with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency awarding Egis Projects UK Ltd a 133.23-million-pound ($181.9m) contract for enforcement services across Britain. Egis businesses also hold UK public contracts, including Galson Sciences, Helios Technology, Egis Transport Solutions and architecture practice WestonWilliamson+Partners.

CAF: Constructing project to continue into 2027

Spanish train manufacturer CAF is also involved in Jerusalem’s light-rail network. The company has disclosed that the 1.8-billion-euro ($2.10bn) Jerusalem project was awarded in 2019 to TransJerusalem J-Net Ltd, a firm owned 50 percent by CAF and 50 percent by Israeli construction business Shapir.

CAF said the project includes construction of the Green Line and extension of the existing Red Line, “which partially run through East Jerusalem”. The construction phase is expected to continue until 2027.

The UN identifies CAF over the “supply of equipment and materials facilitating the construction and the expansion of settlements” and the “use of natural resources, in particular water and land, for business purposes”.

Al Jazeera contacted CAF for comment but received no response.

Meanwhile, CAF has an extensive relationship with Britain’s public sector, including supplying trams for one of the country’s major urban networks. The West Midlands Combined Authority awarded CAF an 83.5-million-pound ($114m) contract for a new generation of trams for the West Midlands Metro. The contract runs until December 2027, according to Tussell data.

Chinese conglomerate Fosun International is identified by the UN under the category covering the commercial use of natural resources, particularly water and land.

Its connection to the occupied West Bank centres on Israeli cosmetics manufacturer Ahava Dead Sea Laboratories. Fosun itself announced in April 2016 that it had agreed to acquire Ahava for 290 million shekels ($76.8m).

Fosun’s subsequent statutory reporting recorded Ahava as 99.46-percent owned.

A European Commission statement in 2018 said Ahava “does have operations in the settlement Mitzpeh Shalem, located in Occupied Territories”.

According to the Quaker-founded organisation, American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), repeated site visits confirmed that Ahava’s former factory in the illegal Mitzpe Shalem settlement remained operational as of 2026.

The group said Dead Sea mud was excavated in the occupied Palestinian territory and initially processed at the site before being transferred to Ein Gedi for further production.

In Britain, Breas Medical, which is ultimately owned through Shanghai Fosun Pharmaceutical by Fosun International, holds two public-sector contracts worth 1.29 million pounds ($1.76m). Fosun International is the controlling shareholder of Shanghai Fosun Pharmaceutical.

Al Jazeera contacted Fosun for comment but received no response.

articles.title: Shootings surge as drug gangs torment Brussels
articles.summary: This year alone there have been more than 65 shootings in the Belgian capital, as drug crime soars.
articles.body:
Last Monday night, drug gangs turned Salvatore's pizzeria in Brussels into a crime scene.

"We dropped to the floor. I had clients eating on the terrace with children. Look, we can see the bullet impacts everywhere."

His restaurant sits on a pretty little square in St Gilles. It's a central area of the city, close to the international Midi train station, where passengers arrive on trains from London and Paris.

Shootings related to drug trafficking have become routine in the Belgian capital over the past couple of years. There were over 100 in 2025 alone, and more than 65 shootings so far this year.

This was the third shooting in this neighbourhood in just three days.

"Are we in an American gangster movie? This needs to stop," Salvatore says.

A suspected drug dealer was shot in the leg in the same area the day before.

Now Murielle and her dog Chéva are sitting at that exact spot, just across the street: "We can still see the trace of the pool of blood."

Murielle is 70, and hopes peace soon returns to her street.

"I like it here. It's like a little village inside the city. Even the drug dealers used to be polite and decent. I would just tell them to go further away and they'd say, 'Yes, ok mama!'"

Drug dealing is happening in plain sight here. Only five minutes after I arrive, I witness a transaction.

A buyer walks up to the seller, shakes their hand, and walks away with the drugs. Crack has become widely consumed amongst the poorest in this area of Brussels.

"Things have changed in the past six months," says Murielle. "The business has intensified. Sometimes you even see consumers queuing to buy drugs. And now gangs are fighting over this spot."

A successful drug-dealing point in Brussels nets up to €50,000 ($58,000; £43,000) per day or more for the dealer, according to the chief of Brussels South Police, Jurgen de Landsheer.

Organised crime in the Belgian capital has become significantly more violent, he says.

At the heart of it all is money. There are more than 200 drug-dealing points across the city, according to the police.

The rise of drug-related violence in the Belgian capital echoes the situation of other European cities such as the French port of Marseille.

Cocaine has become widely available in Europe, the continent's ports serving as entry points for the drug. The port of Antwerp, just 40km (25 miles) away, has seen record cocaine seizures in recent years.

Jurgen de Landsheer says gangs in Brussels are now adopting methods seen in Marseille, although he insists his city has not reached the same level of violence.

"We don't have no-go zones here in Brussels. It's not easy to go in some neighbourhoods, but we go everywhere. We don't want to become like some neighbourhoods in Marseille, so we'll do everything to stop it."

A police station even came under attack last weekend.

CCTV footage shows two men on a scooter stopping in front of the building and shooting at the door several times with what looks like an AK-47 before leaving on their scooter.

This marks an escalation, as it is the first time criminals have targeted police. Usually, the shootings involve rival gangs.

"We see a lot of young people getting paid a few hundred euros. They get a weapon, AK-47 or other heavy weapon, and then they get a mission. To shoot a person in the leg, for example, or to try to kill somebody. And they get very little money for this."

De Landsheer says some of the people his men arrest are as young as 12, and that makes it very dangerous for the whole community.

The spike in shootings has forced Belgian authorities to react and, on Thursday, Belgium's interior minister announced that an extra 40 police officers would be deployed in the problem area.

Jurgen de Landsheer is aware that police alone will not solve this crisis.

"There is no magic solution. We need prevention over repression. We can do our part and be present in the street, but our society also needs to give a future to the young people, do something with them. That's the social part."

Back in St Gilles, Salvatore says it's time for the violence to end.

"Nobody sleeps here at the moment. People talk about moving out, houses are losing value."

Murielle wants to believe that the worst is now behind.

"We will not be intimidated. We'll carry on living and we'll keep on protecting our lovely neighbourhood."

articles.title: MV San Pawl sailings suspended after engine failure
articles.summary: Engineers are carrying out a full assessment of the vessel to establish the extent of the fault.
articles.body:
Passenger sailings between Jersey and Guernsey have been suspended after a major technical failure on the MV San Pawl's starboard main engine.

Operator Islands Unlimited said services would not run until further notice while engineers carried out a full assessment of the vessel and worked to establish the extent of the fault.

The San Pawl is used for foot passenger crossings between the islands and earlier this year successfully completed trials to test whether it could also operate services to Alderney.

The company said the suspension had been introduced to ensure the safety of passengers, crew and the vessel.

Operations manager Jack Kitching said: "We truly regret this disruption to our service, particularly at the peak of our summer season.

"We deeply sympathise with our passengers whose plans have been impacted by this technical failure on board the vessel."

He added: "We are working hard to provide alternative travel arrangements where available and appreciate your patience."

The company said further updates would be issued as soon as more information was available.

articles.title: The Dalit enigma: Why Mayawati is going solo in Punjab
articles.summary: India News: Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) chief Mayawati has decided to go solo in the upcoming 2027 Punjab assembly election. This move has put the spotlight on a st.
articles.body: Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) chief Mayawati has decided to go solo in the upcoming 2027 Punjab assembly election. This move has put the spotlight on a striking contradiction in the state's politics: Punjab has India's highest proportion of Scheduled Castes, but no political party has been able to turn that numerical strength into a durable Dalit vote bloc.On August 25, Mayawati announced that the BSP would contest the polls "alone without any alliance or compromise with anyone", arguing that electoral tie-ups risked weakening the party’s vote share and demoralising its cadre.The decision carries particular significance in Punjab, where BSP founder Kanshi Ram began his political journey and where Scheduled Castes account for 31.94% of the population, according to the 2011 Census.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Yet nearly one-third of Punjab's population has never translated into nearly one-third of the vote for the BSP - or any other Dalit-centric political formation.Instead, the Dalit electorate has remained divided across caste, religious, regional and economic lines, allowing the Congress, AAP, SAD and BJP to each build pockets of support within it.That makes Mayawati's 2027 gamble less about the size of Punjab's Dalit population and more about a difficult political question: Can she turn the state's 32% Dalit population into a coherent electoral bloc?Punjab's number paradoxThe numbers explain why every major political party wants a share of the Dalit vote.Punjab had about 88.6 lakh Scheduled Castes in the 2011 Census, accounting for 31.94% of its population - the highest SC proportion among Indian states. The community is particularly concentrated in the Doaba region, which includes Jalandhar, Hoshiarpur and Nawanshahr.Eight of Doaba's 23 assembly constituencies are reserved for SC candidates, while both Lok Sabha constituencies in the region, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur, are reserved.Across Punjab, 34 of the 117 assembly seats are reserved for Scheduled Caste candidates. But the political influence of Dalit voters extends far beyond these constituencies.A 2021 analysis by Lokniti-CSDS professor Sanjay Kumar found that Dalits accounted for more than 30% of voters in 54 assembly constituencies and between 20% and 30% in another 45.In other words, Dalit voters can influence far more than the 34 seats formally reserved for them.But there is a crucial caveat: 'Dalit' is not a single political identity in Punjab.The community comprises several sub-caste and religious groups, including Ravidassias/Ad-Dharmis, Mazhabi Sikhs, Ramdasias and others. Their geographical distribution, religious affiliations, economic circumstances and political histories differ.That fragmentation has repeatedly prevented the kind of consolidated Dalit politics that emerged around the BSP in Uttar Pradesh.Punjab's agrarian structure adds another layer. Land and economic power remain disproportionately concentrated among dominant agrarian communities, particularly Jat Sikhs. As a result, Dalit politics in the state often revolves around land rights, employment, reservation, social dignity and access to common resources, rather than caste identity alone.From Kanshi Ram's Punjab to BSP's high-water markThe irony is that Punjab was once among the BSP's strongest political laboratories.Kanshi Ram, born in Punjab, built his early political movement around the mobilisation of Scheduled Castes and other marginalised communities before founding the BSP in 1984.The party's breakthrough in Punjab came in the 1992 election. It won nine of the state's 117 seats with 16.32% of the vote, emerging as the principal opposition party in the House. Six of those nine seats came from Doaba, underlining the region’s importance to the party’s political project.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();But the breakthrough proved difficult to sustain.In 1997, the BSP's tally fell to one seat, although it still secured 7.48% of the vote. Its vote share then declined steadily — to 5.69% in 2002, 4.13% in 2007 and 4.29% in 2012. By 2017, it had fallen to 1.52%.In 2022, the BSP won just one seat with 1.77% of the vote, contesting as part of its alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal.The steep decline in three decades captures the central problem Mayawati now faces.How 2022 exposed the paradoxIf the BSP's decline showed the difficulty of sustaining Dalit-centric politics, the 2022 assembly election demonstrated how effectively mainstream parties can cut across caste identities.The AAP won 92 of Punjab's 117 seats with 42.01% of the statewide vote, while Congress was reduced to 18 seats.The AAP’s performance was particularly striking in SC-reserved constituencies. It won 29 of the 34 reserved seats, while Congress won four and the SAD-BSP alliance one.The result also undercut the assumption that Congress's elevation of Charanjit Singh Channi as Punjab's first Dalit CM would automatically consolidate the Dalit vote behind the party. Channi became CM in September 2021, just months before the election. His elevation was widely viewed as an attempt to appeal to the state’s huge Dalit electorate.But in March 2022, Congress suffered a dramatic defeat.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();SAD and its alliance routeThe SAD has historically had its own Dalit support base, particularly among Sikh Dalits.Its alliance with Mayawati ahead of the 2022 election was an attempt to combine the Akali network among sections of the Sikh electorate with the BSP's Dalit support base.The combination, however, failed to produce the revival the two parties had hoped for. The alliance won four seats - three for the SAD and one for the BSP - with a combined vote share of around 20%.BJP's gamble: From alliance politics to going soloThe BJP faces perhaps the most difficult social-coalition challenge of all.Its long-standing electoral arrangement with the SAD ended after the Akali Dal walked out of the NDA at the Centre over the farm laws.The BJP is now trying to establish itself as an independent force in a state where it historically relied heavily on the Akali alliance to provide it with a rural and Sikh social base. That means the party needs to build coalitions beyond the constituencies it traditionally relied on, while also trying to repair its relationship with farmers.Dalit voters are an obvious part of that expansion strategy.But Punjab is not Uttar Pradesh or Bihar. There, the BJP has invested heavily in a social coalition involving non-Yadav OBCs and Dalits. A different caste and religious configuration shapes Punjab’s political landscape, while its agrarian structure and Sikh identity make the BJP’s social engineering considerably more complicated.For the BJP, winning Dalit voters is therefore not simply about adding another community to its support base. It is about constructing an entirely new political coalition in a state where its old alliance no longer provides the same electoral cushion.AAP's pitch: Welfare, not identityThe AAP has already demonstrated why the size of the Dalit population does not automatically translate into BSP votes.In 2022, the party's appeal cut across caste lines, combining welfare, anti-incumbency and the promise of an alternative to the traditional parties. It also had the 'Delhi model' to demonstrate its pitch.AAP sought to build a political vocabulary around BR Ambedkar, combining Ambedkarite symbolism with a broader welfare narrative.Rather than presenting Dalits as a separate electoral constituency, the party has sought to fold their concerns into a larger promise around government schools, healthcare, jobs, welfare delivery and social dignity.However, now the 2027 election will test whether AAP can retain that support after a full term in government.Congress has history, but not the Dalit lockCongress has historically had a strong base among both Hindu and Sikh Dalits in Punjab, but its 2022 performance showed the limits of that advantage. In the 2017 election, the party won 21 of 34 SC-reserved seats; by 2022, after making Charanjit Singh Channi the state’s first Dalit CM and projecting him as its CM face, Congress was reduced to just four reserved seats, while AAP won 29.The setback has not ended Congress's Dalit outreach. In January 2026, Channi himself raised questions within the party over the representation of Dalit leaders, pointing out that several key Punjab Congress positions were held by Jat Sikhs.For Congress, the 2027 challenge is therefore not winning Dalit votes from scratch, but rebuilding a social coalition it once had, without reducing Dalit politics to the Channi factor alone.Mayawati's real gambleMayawati’s decision to contest alone is therefore both ideological and organisational.The BSP has something only a few parties can claim: a political vocabulary explicitly built around Ambedkar, Kanshi Ram and Bahujan mobilisation. Punjab also provides the demographic foundation for such a project.But the party’s electoral history demonstrates the enormous gap between having a potential social constituency and converting it into votes and seats.The challenge is not simply to persuade Dalits to vote for the BSP. It is to persuade different Dalit communities that their interests are sufficiently common to vote for the same party. That is a much harder proposition in Punjab than the 32% figure suggests.Ready to play a spoilsport?There is, however, another reason Mayawati’s decision could matter even if the BSP does not return to anything close to its 1992 performance.Punjab’s 2027 contest is shaping up as a fragmented battle involving AAP, Congress, BJP and SAD, although the possibility of a BJP-SAD reunion remains open.In such a contest, even a relatively small but geographically concentrated BSP vote could become consequential.The party’s past performance offers a warning to the larger parties. In 2024, the BSP was reported to have remained a significant factor in parts of Doaba despite its shrinking statewide base, with observers pointing to its potential to influence contests in seats such as Anandpur Sahib, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur.That is the paradox of Mayawati's Punjab gamble.The BSP may no longer have the numbers to dominate Punjab’s Dalit politics, but it could still have enough votes to disrupt everyone else’s arithmetic.The 2027 election will therefore test not just whether Mayawati can revive the BSP in Kanshi Ram’s home state, but whether Punjab’s nearly 32% Dalit population can finally translate its demographic weight into political leverage - if not as a single bloc, then as the constituency no major party can afford to ignore.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
